chunks.section: Direction or Magnitude? Learning Scalars over Task-Calibrated Directions
chunks.text: Ziqing Wen Xiaohui Song Jiahuan Wang Ping Luo Junlin Zeng Dongsheng Li Kele Xu Tao Sun

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR , which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. The combination of adaptation quality, a compact trainable state, and training efficiency makes SCALAR a promising approach to resource-constrained fine-tuning. 1 1 footnotetext: Work done during an internship at OPPO AI-Center. 1 1 footnotetext: National University of Defense Technology. Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong general-purpose performance, but full-parameter fine-tuning incurs substantial training memory and optimization costs. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) alleviates these costs by updating a small subset of parameters, with LoRA Hu et al. (2022) serving as a widely adopted baseline. For an m × n m\times n linear layer, LoRA optimizes R ⁡ ( m + n ) R(m+n) parameters together with their gradients and optimizer states. These costs are especially relevant to on-device personalization, where local model updates must operate within limited memory and compute budgets. Retaining adaptation quality with a smaller trainable state, lower peak memory, and higher throughput can make such local updates more practical. Recent methods further reduce the optimization budget by learning compact coefficients over fixed bases Bałazy et al. (2024) ; Kopiczko et al. (2024) ; Koohpayegani et al. (2024) ; Albert et al. (2025) . Their effectiveness depends on both the choice of update directions and the computation required to apply them. Random bases provide inexpensive candidate directions, while weight- or activation-derived subspaces use information from pretrained models or downstream data Meng et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2024b) ; Paischer et al. (2025) . Recent evidence also suggests that useful task-improving perturbations can be abundant around pretrained weights Gan and Isola (2026) . These observations motivate the following question.

How can we construct a task-relevant fixed update space that maintains adaptation quality with few trainable coefficients, low memory use, and high throughput? We first investigate this question through a learned-direction reweighting diagnostic. We train a rank-one LoRA adapter, freeze its learned update direction for each adapted matrix, and re-optimize one scalar coefficient per matrix. On a 7B model, the reweighting stage optimizes 196 196 parameters compared with LoRA’s 2,523,136 2{,}523{,}136 , and achieves similar optimization behavior and downstream accuracy. This observation motivates constructing informative directions before fine-tuning and adapting through a small set of coefficients. We propose SCALAR : Subspace-Calibrated Adaptation via Layerwise Atom Reweighting . SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from the leading singular vectors of downstream activations and assigns a separate random output dictionary to each input direction. Learning the coefficients selects an effective output vector within each of these fixed output subspaces. With R R input directions and H H output atoms per direction, each adapted matrix has K = R ​ H K=RH trainable coefficients and an update rank of at most R R . The output atoms in each group are aggregated before application to the activations, so the token-dependent matrix multiplications operate on R R effective directions. Compatible layers can also share the frozen output dictionaries.

Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and code generation show competitive performance with compact trainable budgets. On Qwen2.5-7B and LLaMA3-8B, SCALAR approaches rank-8 LoRA accuracy on commonsense reasoning using about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements demonstrate lower peak training memory and higher throughput, giving the compact parameterization practical value during training. Our analysis builds on activation coverage to examine the initial gradient signal and connects it to the coefficients trained by SCALAR . SCALAR approaches LoRA-level accuracy with substantially fewer trainable parameters. Our main contributions are summarized as follows. Task-calibrated fixed-subspace adaptation. We introduce SCALAR , which combines an activation-derived input basis with a separate random output subspace for each input direction. Its grouped parameterization learns R ​ H RH coefficients and applies the update through R R aggregated output vectors. Compatible layers share their fixed output dictionaries to reduce basis storage. Analysis and diagnostic evidence. Building on activation-subspace analysis, we characterize the effect of gradient-weighted activation geometry on the initial learning signal and derive its connection to SCALAR ’s coefficients. A learned-direction reweighting diagnostic motivates adaptation within informative fixed update spaces.

Competitive performance and training efficiency. SCALAR achieves competitive adaptation performance with substantially fewer trainable parameters across commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and general-domain knowledge evaluation. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show lower peak training memory and higher throughput than LoRA, NOLA, and RandLoRA. Structural ablations examine the benefits of grouped computation and shared output dictionaries. The experiments cover three model families and multiple parameter scales up to 32B, with additional large-model evaluations in the Appendix.

We motivate SCALAR through a learned-direction reweighting diagnostic and an analysis of input subspaces. The diagnostic examines adaptation through scalar coefficients after informative directions have been obtained. The analysis then connects dominant activation directions to input coverage and the initial gradient signal, providing the basis for constructing a fixed input subspace before fine-tuning.

They motivate the practical design of SCALAR , which constructs its input directions from activation statistics before fine-tuning and learns coefficients within the resulting fixed update space.

SCALAR uses the activation geometry analyzed in Section 3 to construct a fixed input basis. Each input direction is paired with a group of random output atoms, and adaptation learns their combination coefficients. The groups define separate output subspaces while keeping the effective update rank bounded by the number of input directions. This construction keeps the trainable state compact and supports efficient evaluation through a small set of effective output vectors. chunks.text: At zero coefficient initialization, isotropic random output atoms relate the expected scalar-gradient energy to the gradient-weighted activation energy 𝒢 ⁡ ( 𝑨 ) \mathcal{G}(\bm{A}) . The covariance-alignment condition connects this quantity to activation coverage. Appendix A.3 provides the derivation for the trainable coefficients. Each adapted layer maintains its own activation-derived basis 𝑨 \bm{A} and trainable coefficient matrix 𝚪 \bm{\Gamma} . Layers of the same module type with compatible output dimensions may share the fixed output dictionaries { 𝑩 r } r = 1 R \{\bm{B}_{r}\}_{r=1}^{R} . Layer-specific input bases and coefficients produce distinct updates from the shared atoms. The sharing ablation in Appendix C.6.1 shows lower memory consumption with similar accuracy. The construction reduces three sources of training cost. Learning only the coefficient set reduces gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped evaluation limits token-dependent adapter computation, while dictionary sharing reduces the memory occupied by fixed output bases. Section 5.2 reports the resulting peak memory and throughput measurements. These properties are useful for on-device personalization under limited memory and compute budgets.

We evaluate adaptation quality at compact trainable budgets and measure the corresponding training memory and throughput. The experiments cover several language adaptation tasks. The Appendix includes additional diagnostic analyses, comparisons with enhanced LoRA variants, general instruction fine-tuning, larger-model evaluations, and extensive ablations on the parameterization, calibration, rank, initialization, and cross-layer sharing, together with full implementation details and parameter-budget comparisons. Training Configuration. We evaluate SCALAR on commonsense reasoning with Qwen2.5 Yang et al. (2024a) and LLaMA3 Grattafiori et al. (2024) , and further test transfer to mathematical reasoning and code generation. We also ablate the initialization of the fixed bases 𝑨 \bm{A} and 𝑩 \bm{B} . Baselines. We compare SCALAR with full-parameter fine-tuning and five representative PEFT methods: Full Fine-tuning (FT) as a full-capacity reference; LoRA Hu et al. (2022) , the standard trainable low-rank parameterization; VeRA Kopiczko et al. (2024) , which shares random low-rank projections and learns layer-specific scaling vectors; LoRA-XS Bałazy et al. (2024) , which optimizes a compact matrix between fixed projections; NOLA Koohpayegani et al. (2024) , which learns combinations of fixed random bases; and RandLoRA Albert et al. (2025) , which aggregates random low-rank bases with trainable diagonal scalings.

We present the main accuracy results in Table 3 and the parameter–performance comparison in Figure 1 . We fine-tune all methods on the Commonsense170K training set Hu et al. (2023) and evaluate on 8 commonsense reasoning benchmarks. We conduct experiments on both LLaMA3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, and report the mean accuracy over three independent runs. A more comprehensive comparison covering multiple trainable-parameter budgets for NOLA, LoRA-XS, and the other PEFT baselines is provided in Appendix Table 10 . Parameter Efficiency. Table 3 shows that SCALAR approaches LoRA-level accuracy with substantially smaller trainable budgets. With K = 4096 K=4096 , it reaches 88.9 average accuracy on Qwen2.5-7B and 87.3 on LLaMA3-8B, compared with 88.8 and 87.4 for rank-8 LoRA. We investigate the effects of different initialization strategies for the input-side basis 𝑨 \bm{A} and the output-side dictionary 𝑩 \bm{B} . As shown in Table 5 , activation-SVD consistently yields the strongest initialization for 𝑨 \bm{A} , outperforming both random and weight-SVD initialization under either choice of 𝑩 \bm{B} . This result supports our design of extracting 𝑨 \bm{A} from the dominant activation subspace, which better captures the downstream input geometry. Random output atoms additionally support sharing across compatible layers, reducing the storage of layer-specific output bases as examined in Appendix C.6.1 . We therefore use activation-SVD 𝑨 \bm{A} and random, shareable 𝑩 \bm{B} as the default construction.

We introduced SCALAR , a PEFT method that combines competitive adaptation performance with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. The method learns layer-specific scalar coefficients over activation-derived input directions and grouped random output dictionaries. Compact coefficient updates reduce the trainable state, grouped evaluation limits token-dependent computation, and shared dictionaries reduce fixed-basis storage. Our analysis relates the task-calibrated input geometry to the initial learning signal, while the experiments and structural ablations demonstrate its parameter and training efficiency. These properties make SCALAR a promising approach for on-device personalization under limited memory and compute budgets.

This section supplements Section 4 with implementation details, training hyperparameters, baseline implementations, and the complete commonsense reasoning results. Unless stated otherwise, all implementation choices are shared across methods whenever their parameterizations permit.

We summarize the main implementation choices used in our experiments. Notation follows Section 4 . For each adapted layer, SCALAR maintains a task-aware input matrix 𝑨 ∈ ℝ R × n \bm{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times n} and a trainable coefficient matrix 𝚪 ∈ ℝ R × H \bm{\Gamma}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times H} , where R R controls the maximum rank of the aggregated update and H H is the number of random output atoms per input direction. The random output dictionaries { 𝑩 r } r = 1 R \{\bm{B}_{r}\}_{r=1}^{R} are frozen and may be shared across layers with the same module type. Coefficient-only optimization keeps adapter gradients and optimizer states compact. Grouping reuses each input projection across its output atoms, reducing token-dependent work. Cross-layer sharing limits the resident storage of the frozen output dictionaries.

chunks.section: B.1.1 Optional Sharing of Output Dictionaries
chunks.text: Because the output atoms are sampled independently of pretrained weights, compatible layers may reuse the same frozen dictionaries { 𝑩 r } r = 1 R \{\bm{B}_{r}\}_{r=1}^{R} . For example, query-projection layers with the same output dimension can reuse one dictionary while retaining their own activation-derived 𝑨 \bm{A} and trainable 𝚪 \bm{\Gamma} . We detail the hyperparameters used to reproduce our experimental results. All methods are optimized with AdamW using β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 , and ϵ = 1 ​ e − 8 \epsilon=1\mathrm{e}{-8} . We use BF16 precision to reduce memory consumption and train with Distributed Data Parallel (DDP). Gradient synchronization is implemented using PyTorch’s Paszke et al. [2017] torch.distributed framework. Following a widely used configuration for LLM adaptation, we apply all PEFT methods to the same set of Transformer linear layers. chunks.section: C.3 Comparison with Enhanced LoRA Variants
chunks.text: We further compare SCALAR with DoRA Liu et al. [2024] , PiSSA Meng et al. [2024] , and EVA Paischer et al. [2025] , which represent three complementary improvements over standard LoRA. EVA is particularly relevant because it also exploits activation geometry; however, unlike EVA, which subsequently trains both LoRA factors, SCALAR freezes the activation-derived input basis and learns only scalar combinations of fixed random output atoms. All methods are evaluated on Qwen2.5-7B using the same training and evaluation protocol. chunks.section: C.6.1 Grouped Parameterization and Cross-Layer Sharing
chunks.text: Grouped parameterization. As introduced in Section 4 , SCALAR parameterizes the weight update as Δ ​ 𝑾 = s ​ ∑ r = 1 R ∑ h = 1 H γ r , h ​ 𝒃 r , h ​ 𝒂 r ⊤ , K = R ​ H , \Delta\bm{W}=s\sum_{r=1}^{R}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\gamma_{r,h}\bm{b}_{r,h}\bm{a}_{r}^{\top},\qquad K=RH, where the H H components in each group share the same input-side direction 𝒂 r \bm{a}_{r} , while retaining distinct output-side directions 𝒃 r , h \bm{b}_{r,h} . The update can therefore be equivalently expressed as Δ ​ 𝑾 = s ​ ∑ r = 1 R 𝒃 ~ r ​ 𝒂 r ⊤ , 𝒃 ~ r = ∑ h = 1 H γ r , h ​ 𝒃 r , h . \Delta\bm{W}=s\sum_{r=1}^{R}\widetilde{\bm{b}}_{r}\bm{a}_{r}^{\top},\qquad\widetilde{\bm{b}}_{r}=\sum_{h=1}^{H}\gamma_{r,h}\bm{b}_{r,h}. (10) Although the formulation contains K = R ​ H K=RH scalar-weighted atoms, the H H output atoms within each group can be merged into a single effective output vector 𝒃 ~ r \widetilde{\bm{b}}_{r} before being applied to the input activations. Consequently, the resulting update has rank at most R R , rather than K K . This grouped structure also reduces the cost of applying the update. For a batch of activations 𝑿 ∈ ℝ n × L \bm{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times L} , where L L denotes the total number of tokens, the grouped update can be evaluated as Δ ​ 𝑾 ​ 𝑿 = s ​ 𝑩 ~ ​ 𝑨 ​ 𝑿 , \Delta\bm{W}\bm{X}=s\widetilde{\bm{B}}\bm{A}\bm{X}, where 𝑨 ∈ ℝ R × n \bm{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times n} and 𝑩 ~ ∈ ℝ m × R \widetilde{\bm{B}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times R} . Constructing 𝑩 ~ \widetilde{\bm{B}} requires weighted accumulation of the K K fixed output atoms, with cost 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ​ K ) \mathcal{O}(mK) . The subsequent matrix multiplications cost 𝒪 ⁡ ( L ​ R ​ ( n + m ) ) \mathcal{O}(LR(n+m)) , giving a total complexity of 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ​ K + L ​ R ​ ( n + m ) ) . \mathcal{O}\bigl(mK+LR(n+m)\bigr).

chunks.text: Since K = R ​ H K=RH , the token-dependent matrix-multiplication cost scales with R R rather than K K . To examine the structural trade-off between the number of distinct input directions and the per-token computation, we compare the grouped parameterization with an ungrouped variant at the same coefficient budget: Δ ​ 𝑾 = s ​ ∑ k = 1 K γ k ​ 𝒃 k ​ 𝒂 k ⊤ , \Delta\bm{W}=s\sum_{k=1}^{K}\gamma_{k}\bm{b}_{k}\bm{a}_{k}^{\top}, (11) where each scalar coefficient is associated with an independent pair of input- and output-side directions. At this coefficient budget, the grouped and ungrouped variants obtain average accuracies of 88.5 88.5 and 88.3 88.3 , respectively. The grouped variant combines comparable accuracy with higher throughput by allocating K K output atoms across R R input directions. The coefficient budget is unchanged, while the grouped computation applies fewer distinct input and output projections to each token. This comparison shows the system benefit of organizing the dictionary for efficient application. Cross-layer sharing of B \bm{B} . We next examine the cross-layer sharing strategy for the output-side bases. In the default implementation, layers corresponding to the same projection module share the same collection of fixed output directions { 𝒃 r , h } \{\bm{b}_{r,h}\} . For example, all query-projection layers reuse one output basis, while different module types retain separate bases. Layer-specific adaptation is still preserved because each layer learns its own coefficients γ r , h \gamma_{r,h} .

We evaluate the adaptation methods on three representative domains: commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. For each domain, we fine-tune the pretrained models on a corresponding instruction dataset and evaluate the resulting checkpoints on held-out benchmarks. The descriptions below summarize the data used in our experiments; evaluation details and hyperparameters are given in Appendix B.2 .

• Commonsense170K. Commonsense170K Hu et al. [2023] is a collection of approximately 170K instruction-formatted examples constructed from the training sets of eight commonsense reasoning benchmarks: BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and OpenBookQA. The original tasks are converted into a unified instruction–response format and combined for multi-task fine-tuning. Following prior PEFT studies, we train on the combined dataset and evaluate separately on the test set of each constituent benchmark. • MetaMathQA. MetaMathQA Yu et al. [2023] is a mathematical instruction-tuning dataset containing approximately 395K examples. It is constructed by rewriting existing mathematical questions from multiple perspectives, including forward, backward, and answer-conditioned transformations, while preserving the underlying mathematical knowledge. The dataset contains step-by-step solutions and is designed to improve multi-step mathematical reasoning. We fine-tune the models on MetaMathQA and evaluate them on GSM8K and MATH. • Code-Feedback. Code-Feedback Zheng et al. [2024] contains approximately 66K code-related interactions involving code generation, execution feedback, and iterative refinement. Its examples cover both initial solutions and subsequent corrections based on execution results, providing supervision for generating functionally correct programs. We use Code-Feedback for code instruction tuning and evaluate the resulting models on HumanEval and MBPP.

Commonsense Reasoning. We evaluate commonsense reasoning using the eight benchmarks included in Commonsense170K: • BoolQ Clark et al. [2019] consists of naturally occurring yes-or-no questions paired with passages and evaluates reading comprehension and implicit reasoning. • PIQA Bisk et al. [2020] evaluates physical commonsense reasoning by asking models to select the more plausible solution to an everyday physical problem. • SIQA Sap et al. [2019] contains multiple-choice questions about social interactions and evaluates reasoning about people’s intentions, reactions, and social consequences. • HellaSwag Zellers et al. [2019] evaluates commonsense natural-language inference by requiring models to select the most plausible continuation of a given context. • WinoGrande Sakaguchi et al. [2021] is a large-scale Winograd-style benchmark that tests commonsense reasoning and coreference resolution through binary fill-in-the-blank questions. • ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge Clark et al. [2018] are the easy and challenging subsets of the AI2 Reasoning Challenge, respectively. Both contain grade-school-level multiple-choice science questions, with ARC-Challenge including questions that are more difficult for retrieval- and word-matching-based systems. • OpenBookQA Mihaylov et al. [2018] contains multiple-choice science questions that require combining elementary scientific facts with broader commonsense knowledge. We report accuracy on each benchmark and use their unweighted mean as the overall commonsense reasoning score. Mathematical Reasoning. We evaluate mathematical reasoning on GSM8K and MATH:

• GSM8K Cobbe et al. [2021] contains 8.5K linguistically diverse grade-school mathematics word problems. Solving these problems generally requires several arithmetic reasoning steps before producing a final numerical answer. • MATH Hendrycks et al. [2021b] consists of competition-level mathematics problems spanning algebra, counting and probability, geometry, intermediate algebra, number theory, pre-algebra, and pre-calculus. Compared with GSM8K, it requires more advanced mathematical knowledge and longer reasoning chains. We extract the final answer from each model response and report exact-match accuracy following the standard evaluation protocol. Code Generation. We evaluate code generation on HumanEval and MBPP: • HumanEval Chen et al. [2021] contains 164 hand-written Python programming problems. Each problem provides a function signature, a natural-language specification, and hidden unit tests used to assess functional correctness. • MBPP Austin et al. [2021] contains short Python programming problems described in natural language, together with reference solutions and test cases. The tasks primarily assess the ability to synthesize functionally correct programs for basic programming problems. For both benchmarks, generated programs are executed against the provided unit tests, and we report pass@1 as the primary metric.

General-Domain Knowledge Evaluation. We evaluate post-tuning general-domain knowledge performance using Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) Hendrycks et al. [2021a] . MMLU consists of multiple-choice questions from 57 academic and professional subjects, covering STEM, humanities, social sciences, and other domains. The benchmark evaluates the breadth of a model’s pretrained knowledge and its ability to apply that knowledge across heterogeneous subject areas. We report accuracy for the four aggregated subject categories and the overall accuracy across all MMLU tasks. These scores characterize post-tuning knowledge performance after fine-tuning on Alpaca-GPT4 Peng et al. [2023] .
